title: Evaluating Models
description: Metrics for classification and regression, ROC and precision–recall curves, imbalanced data, calibration, and the uncertainty in an evaluation.
overview: A model is only as good as the measurement used to judge it. Accuracy, the fraction of correct predictions, looks natural and is often misleading: a model that always predicts the majority class can be 99% accurate on rare-disease data and useless. The right metric depends on what mistakes cost.

This chapter introduces the standard metrics, the curves that show a classifier across all its thresholds, the treatment of imbalanced classes and probability calibration, and the statistics of how much an estimate of performance can be trusted.
objectives: Compute accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1 from a confusion matrix, and choose among them for a given problem.
Construct an ROC curve and compute AUC, and explain its probabilistic meaning.
Handle imbalanced classes with appropriate metrics, weights and thresholds.
Compute and interpret MSE, RMSE, MAE and R² for regression, and log loss and calibration for probabilistic predictions.
Put a confidence interval on a test-set accuracy and decide how large a test set must be.

sections.title: The confusion matrix and its metrics
body: For a binary classifier with a positive and a negative class, every prediction falls into one of four cells.

eqs: fraction of all predictions that are correct
of the examples called positive, the fraction that are
of the actual positives, the fraction found
of the actual negatives, the fraction correctly rejected
harmonic mean of precision P and recall R

body: Precision answers: when the model raises an alarm, how often is it right? Recall answers: how many of the real cases does it catch? They pull against each other. A model that flags everything has perfect recall and poor precision, and a model that flags only the most certain cases has high precision and poor recall. The F1 score is the harmonic mean, which stays low unless both are high. To see why it is used instead of the ordinary average, take a model with precision 1.0 and recall 0.1. The ordinary average is 0.55, which sounds respectable for a model that finds only 1 real case in 10. The F1 score is 2(1.0)(0.1)/(1.0 + 0.1) = 0.18, which reflects how poor the model is.

A way to keep the four cells straight: the second word says what the model said (positive or negative), and the first word says whether it was right. A //false positive// is a wrong "positive" call, a false alarm. A //false negative// is a wrong "negative" call, a miss.

example.title: A disease screening test
example.problem: Of 1000 patients, 60 have the disease. The test gives TP = 40, FN = 20, FP = 10, TN = 930. Compute accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1. Compare accuracy with a rule that always says healthy.
solution: The always-healthy rule has TP = 0 and TN = 940, so its accuracy is 940/1000 = 0.94. The test's 0.97 looks like a small gain over it, but the test finds two-thirds of the sick patients and the rule finds none. Accuracy hides this; recall exposes it.

list: When a miss is costly (cancer screening, fraud, safety), prioritize **recall** and accept more false alarms.
When a false alarm is costly (blocking a legitimate email, an unnecessary surgery), prioritize **precision**.
When both matter and classes are skewed, use **F1**, or the F-beta score F_β = (1 + β²)PR / (β²P + R), which weights recall β times as much as precision.
With more than two classes, compute the metric per class, then average: **macro** average (each class equal) or **micro** average (each example equal).

check.q: TP = 30, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 140. What is the precision?
check.why: Precision = TP/(TP + FP) = 30/40 = 0.75. Recall would be 30/50 = 0.60.

check.q: A spam filter must almost never block a legitimate email. Which metric should be held high?
wrong: Specificity on the legitimate class can be ignored

sections.title: Thresholds, ROC curves and AUC
body: Most classifiers output a score s(x), such as a probability, and predict positive when s(x) exceeds a **threshold** τ. Moving τ trades false positives for false negatives. The confusion matrix and everything derived from it depend on the choice of τ.

The **ROC curve** (receiver operating characteristic) traces the whole tradeoff. For each threshold it plots the **true positive rate** (TPR = recall) against the **false positive rate** (FPR = FP / (FP + TN) = 1 − specificity). A random classifier gives the diagonal. A perfect one reaches the top-left corner.

body: The **area under the ROC curve** (AUC) summarizes the curve in one number from 0.5 (random) to 1 (perfect). It has a direct meaning: AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen positive example receives a higher score than a randomly chosen negative one. It measures ranking quality and does not depend on any threshold or on the class balance.

example.title: AUC by counting pairs
example.problem: Three positives have scores 0.9, 0.7, 0.4 and three negatives have scores 0.8, 0.3, 0.2. Find the AUC.
solution: There are 3 × 3 = 9 positive–negative pairs. Count those in which the positive scores higher.
Positive 0.9 beats all three negatives (3). Positive 0.7 beats 0.3 and 0.2 but not 0.8 (2). Positive 0.4 beats 0.3 and 0.2 (2).

example.title: Building the ROC curve from the same six scores
example.problem: Use the scores above (positives 0.9, 0.7, 0.4; negatives 0.8, 0.3, 0.2). Trace the ROC curve by lowering the threshold one score at a time.
solution: Sort the examples by score, highest first: 0.9 (positive), 0.8 (negative), 0.7 (positive), 0.4 (positive), 0.3 (negative), 0.2 (negative). Start with a threshold above every score, so nothing is called positive: TPR = 0 and FPR = 0.

Lower the threshold to just under each score in turn. Each time, the example that was just crossed becomes a predicted positive. If it is truly positive, the curve moves up by 1/3 (one of the 3 positives is now found). If it is truly negative, the curve moves right by 1/3 (one of the 3 negatives is now falsely flagged).

solution: Plotting the TPR and FPR columns gives the curve in the figure. The area under it is the same 7/9 found by counting pairs. A curve that climbs steeply at first means the highest-scored examples are mostly positive, which is what a good ranking looks like.

body: When positives are rare, the false positive rate can look tiny even when the false positives outnumber the true ones: 100 false alarms among 100,000 negatives is an FPR of 0.001. The **precision–recall curve** plots precision against recall across thresholds and reflects this problem directly. For imbalanced tasks, report the area under the precision–recall curve (average precision) alongside, or instead of, ROC AUC.

The curve gives the options, but a deployed model uses one threshold. Select it from the cost of each kind of error. If a false negative costs c_FN and a false positive costs c_FP, the best threshold on a calibrated probability p is to predict positive when p > c_FP / (c_FP + c_FN).

sections.title: Imbalanced classes
body: Fraud, defects, rare diseases and clicks on ads all have a positive class that is a tiny fraction of the data. Three things go wrong with default practice.

list: Accuracy rewards ignoring the minority class.
Training objectives, which average over examples, are dominated by the majority class, so the model has little incentive to find the minority.

Metrics such as precision depend on the **base rate** (the share of positives). A test with 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity for a disease that affects 1 in 1000 people has a precision of only about 9%.

example.title: Why a good test gives mostly false alarms
example.problem: A disease has prevalence 0.1%. A test has sensitivity 0.99 and specificity 0.99. Of 100,000 people, how many test positive, and what fraction of those are sick?
solution: There are 100 sick people and 99,900 healthy people. True positives: 0.99 × 100 = 99. False positives: 0.01 × 99,900 = 999.
About 91% of positive results are false alarms, because healthy people so greatly outnumber sick people. This is Bayes' rule at work (see Probability).

list: **Use the right metrics**: precision, recall, F1 and average precision, not accuracy.
**Class weights**: multiply the loss on minority examples by a weight, usually the inverse class frequency. This changes what the objective rewards without touching the data.
**Resampling**: oversample the minority class (duplicate or synthesize examples) or undersample the majority. Resample only the training folds, never the validation or test data.
**Move the threshold**: train normally, then choose the threshold on a validation set to reach the target precision or recall.
**Collect more minority examples**, or use anomaly detection when positives are too rare to learn from.

body.warn: If you reweight or resample the classes, the predicted probabilities no longer match the real base rate. Recalibrate them before using the numbers as probabilities.

check.q: Why does precision fall as a condition becomes rarer, with sensitivity and specificity fixed?
check.a: The false positives come from a much larger group of negatives

sections.title: Regression and probabilistic metrics
body: For a regression model with predictions ŷ_i and targets y_i over m examples:

eqs: mean squared error; penalizes large errors heavily
mean absolute error; less sensitive to outliers
fraction of the variance of y that the model explains

body: R² compares the model with the baseline that always predicts the mean ȳ. R² = 1 is perfect, R² = 0 matches the baseline, and R² can be negative on held-out data when the model is worse than the baseline.

example.title: Regression metrics
example.problem: Targets are 3, 5, 7, 9 and predictions are 2.5, 5.5, 6.5, 9.5. Compute MSE, RMSE, MAE and R².
solution: The errors are all ±0.5, so squared errors sum to 4(0.25) = 1.

body: Many classifiers output a probability p̂ that the label is 1. The **log loss** (cross-entropy) scores the probabilities themselves. For each example it takes the probability the model gave to the //correct// label and charges the negative logarithm of it: nothing if that probability was 1, and a rapidly growing penalty as it approaches 0. Averaged over the data:

body.eq: log loss = −(1/m) Σ [ y_i ln p̂_i + (1 − y_i) ln(1 − p̂_i) ]

body: A confident wrong answer is punished severely: with y = 1, p̂ = 0.8 costs −ln 0.8 = 0.223, while y = 0 with p̂ = 0.8 costs −ln 0.2 = 1.609. The **Brier score** is the mean squared error between p̂ and the 0/1 outcome and is bounded, which makes it less sensitive to extreme errors.

A model is **calibrated** if, among all examples assigned probability p̂, a fraction p̂ are in fact positive. A weather forecast that says 70% on days when it rains 70% of the time is calibrated. Plot the observed frequency against the predicted probability in bins to see the **reliability diagram**. Calibration matters whenever the probability feeds a decision. Overconfident networks can be fixed with a one-parameter rescaling (temperature scaling) or isotonic regression fit on validation data.

sections.title: How sure is the estimate?
body: A test-set accuracy is itself an estimate from a finite sample. If the true accuracy is p and the m test examples are independent, the number of correct predictions is Binomial(m, p), and the observed accuracy p̂ has standard error
An approximate 95% confidence interval is p̂ ± 1.96 SE.

example.title: Confidence interval for accuracy
example.problem: A model classifies 340 of 400 test examples correctly. Give a 95% confidence interval for its accuracy, and find how many test examples are needed for a half-width of 1% when the accuracy is near 0.90.

body: This calculation explains why differences of a percentage point between two models on a few hundred test examples mean nothing. When comparing two models, test them on the same examples and look at the examples where they disagree; a paired test, such as McNemar's test, uses only those. Repeating training with different random seeds and splits shows a second source of variance, in the model itself.

list: **Grid search** tries every combination from a fixed grid. **Random search** samples combinations at random, and is more efficient when only a few hyperparameters matter, because it tries more distinct values of each.
Search learning rates and penalty strengths on a log scale.
Always compare against a simple baseline, and against the same model with one component removed (an **ablation**) to see what each part contributes.
Do **error analysis**: read a sample of the mistakes, group them, and fix the largest group. This is usually more productive than another round of tuning.
Check that evaluation data resemble deployment data. A model evaluated on last year's customers may fail on this year's; this is **distribution shift**.
Evaluate by subgroup. An overall metric can hide a group for which the model is much worse; fairness metrics compare error rates across groups.

check.q: How does the standard error of accuracy change if the test set grows by a factor of 4?
wrong: It falls by a factor of 4

summary: The confusion matrix gives accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1. Choose the metric that matches the cost of each kind of error; accuracy misleads on imbalanced data.
ROC curves plot TPR against FPR over all thresholds. AUC is the probability that a random positive outranks a random negative. Precision–recall curves are better for rare positives.
With imbalance, use class weights, resampling of training data and a tuned threshold. Precision depends on the base rate.
MSE, RMSE, MAE and R² evaluate regression. Log loss and Brier score evaluate probabilities, and calibration checks that probabilities mean what they say.
A test metric is an estimate with a standard error of about √(p(1 − p)/m). Small differences on small test sets are noise.
Use baselines, ablations, error analysis and subgroup checks.

problems.q: A classifier produces TP = 45, FP = 15, FN = 5, TN = 135. Compute accuracy, precision, recall and F1.
Positives have scores 0.95, 0.6, 0.55 and negatives have scores 0.7, 0.5, 0.3, 0.1. Compute the AUC.
problems.solution: There are 3 × 4 = 12 pairs. Positive 0.95 beats all 4. Positive 0.6 beats 0.5, 0.3, 0.1 (3) but not 0.7. Positive 0.55 beats 0.5, 0.3, 0.1 (3). Total 10, so AUC = 10/12.

problems.q: A fraud rate is 0.5%. A detector has recall 0.80 and false positive rate 0.02. Of 200,000 transactions, how many are flagged, and what is the precision?
problems.solution: Fraudulent: 1000; legitimate: 199,000. True positives: 0.80 × 1000 = 800. False positives: 0.02 × 199,000 = 3980. Flagged: 4780. Precision = 800/4780.

problems.q: A model scores 0.78 accuracy on a test set of 250. Give an approximate 95% confidence interval. Can you conclude it beats a model with 0.75 accuracy?
problems.solution: SE = √(0.78 × 0.22/250) = √(0.0006864) = 0.0262. The interval is 0.78 ± 0.051, or [0.729, 0.831]. It contains 0.75, so the data do not show that the model is better.
problems.a: [0.73, 0.83]; no, the difference is within the noise.

problems.q: For labels 1 and 0 with predicted probabilities 0.9 and 0.4, compute the log loss.
problems.solution: The losses are −ln 0.9 = 0.105 for the first example and −ln(1 − 0.4) = −ln 0.6 = 0.511 for the second. The mean is (0.105 + 0.511)/2 = 0.308.
